mechanism: Pick two coins whose prices have moved together (rolling correlation or cointegration on hourly closes). When the spread between them widens, the laggard is expected to catch up with the leader as the spread mean-reverts. Long-only version buys only the laggard and exits when the spread closes or a time stop hits. Numbers come from public exchange candles; the edge has to survive fees and the cases where the pair breaks for good.
claim: The reel says trading the laggard of a matched pair against the leader gives steady returns.
verdict_question: On public hourly candles for 20 liquid spot pairs, does buying the laggard when the spread passes 2 sigma beat holding it over the next 48 hours after 0.2 percent round-trip fees?
probe_title: Pairs laggard: does the long-only laggard of a matched crypto pair beat holding after 0.2% fees on 90 days of hourly candles?
one_line: A pairs-trading reel claims the laggard catches up; a long-only fee-adjusted replay on public candles will say whether it does.
idea_why: Mean reversion in correlated pairs is real in principle, but costs and permanently broken pairs often erase it, so only a dated replay settles it.
breakdown: Pull 90 days of hourly closes for a list of liquid spot pairs from a keyless exchange or aggregator endpoint. Compute a rolling log-ratio for each candidate pair and its z-score, and fix the entry (z above 2 on the laggard side), exit (z back to 0) and time stop before looking at results. Replay long-only, charge fees on both legs, and compare against simply holding the same coin for the same windows and against random entry dates. Commit the rules and due date first with the preregister skill, then score with the luck-test skill. No hired help needed; the open question is whether pairs break inside the window.

mechanism: An LLM agent normally reasons before every primitive action using the full history. ChunkAct compiles stored memory offline into chains of primitives per sub-goal. At run time one call launches a whole chunk, which runs without the model and hands control back only on failure, so model calls scale with decisions rather than steps.
claim: On LIBERO-Pro it gains 5.0 points in task success with 2.9x fewer LLM calls and 4.4x fewer input tokens.
why_not_testable: It needs the LIBERO-Pro robot simulator and a VLA stack, which are not keyless or quick.
needs: LIBERO-Pro simulator and a vision-language-action model.
one_line: Compile repeated agent routines into chunks that run without the model and return control only on failure: 2.9x fewer calls in a robot benchmark.
idea_why: Replacing repeated model reasoning with compiled routines that escalate only on failure is a general, sensible way to cut agent cost.
breakdown: Log successful agent runs, cluster repeated tool-call sequences per sub-goal, and store them as scripts with a pass/fail check at the end. At run time the planner picks a sub-goal and the script runs unattended, calling the model only if the check fails. The same idea applies to Proteus nightly tasks that repeat the same Bash sequences.

mechanism: A catch-all mail domain accepts any address at receive time. The first sender (domain, or exact address for webmail providers) to write to an address becomes its only allowed sender, and the service rejects all later mail from anyone else. Prefix inboxes let you invent suffixes on the fly, each locking to its first writer, and temporary inboxes expire and bounce. A bounce for unknown senders is what a spammer's list-cleaning sees, and an MCP server lets an AI read the inboxes.
claim: Infinite self-creating inboxes, each locked to one sender, so leaked addresses stop receiving spam.
why_not_testable: It requires signing up for the service and owning a domain.
needs: An account on the service and a domain with MX records.
one_line: Every email address you invent locks to the first sender who uses it, so a leak shows exactly who sold you out.
idea_why: First-sender locking on a catch-all domain is a simple, working way to trace leaks and kill spam per address.
breakdown: Run a catch-all domain with a mail server that records the first envelope sender per recipient and rejects others at SMTP time. Give each service a unique suffix. Self-hosting is a few hours with an existing open source mail server and a rule script.
